Females of Micropogonias undulatus captured during the peak of the reproductive season showed a mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 7% [GSI = 7%] when water temperatures averaged 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The pelagic eggs produced by this species each measure approximately 0.8 millimetres in diameter, and the wet weight of a newly fertilised ovum at the moment of zygote formation is roughly 0.000268 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.000268 grams]. Such a minute initial mass, inferred from the volume of a spherical egg using the standard geometric relationship, places the species among the many marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small, pelagic propagules. The total length of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva remains modest at this stage, and the endogenous nutritional reserves provided by the yolk must sustain the larva through the first days of development until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding becomes possible.

Laboratory-based growth studies conducted under controlled thermal conditions revealed that Micropogonias undulatus displays a pronounced allometric shift in body shape during the transition from the planktonic larval phase to the pelagic-benthic transition of the post-settlement juvenile. Individuals reared at a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] attained a total length of 18 centimetres [Lp = 18 centimetres] at the onset of sexual maturation, a length that coincides with the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and the initiation of gametogenesis. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty, derived from a length-weight relationship fitted to regional samples, is approximately 80.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 80.7 grams]. This relationship indicates that the species shifts from a primarily somatic growth trajectory to one that includes reproductive investment once this length threshold is crossed. The attainment of puberty at this relatively modest size allows individuals to begin contributing to the breeding population at an early age, which may buffer the population against periods of high adult mortality. Such a life-history strategy is common among fast-growing, short-lived sciaenids that inhabit dynamic estuarine environments.

The maximum recorded total length for Micropogonias undulatus in the northern Gulf of Mexico has been established at 55 centimetres [Li = 55 centimetres], a value that represents the ultimate total length achieved by sexually mature adults in this population. Corresponding to this asymptotic length, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual, calculated from the regional length-weight conversion, reaches approximately 2750 grams [Wwi = approximately 2750 grams]. This body mass is consistent with the largest individuals sampled during long-term fishery-independent monitoring surveys. The substantial increase in body size from puberty to the ultimate length allows older, larger females to make a disproportionately large contribution to annual egg production, as fecundity in sciaenids generally scales positively with female body mass. Consequently, the preservation of larger, older individuals within the population is believed to be important for maintaining reproductive output and population resilience, particularly in the face of variable recruitment success that characterises estuarine-dependent species. The growth pattern itself, which decelerates markedly after puberty, follows the typical asymptotic trajectory of a determinate-growing teleost.

Mark-recapture studies and otolith-based ageing have indicated that the maximum lifespan recorded for Micropogonias undulatus in the wild, under the prevailing thermal regime of the northern Gulf of Mexico, is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This longevity was documented in a population exposed to an average annual water temperature near 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a condition that supports relatively slow metabolic ageing compared to more southerly, warmer populations. The species thus appears to exhibit a typical pattern for a medium-sized, iteroparous sciaenid, with a lifespan that allows multiple reproductive seasons over the course of an individual’s life. Such a life span, combined with the early onset of puberty at 18 centimetres [Lp = 18 centimetres] total length, means that individuals have a considerable reproductive window during which they can contribute offspring to the population across several spawning seasons. This extended window may be particularly advantageous in an estuarine environment where year-class strength is highly variable and determined largely by environmental conditions during the early larval period. The preservation of this age structure is a key consideration for fisheries management.

At the temperature typical of the spawning season (20 °C [T = 20 °C]), the gonadosomatic index reaches approximately 7% [GSI = approximately 7%] in actively spawning females. The pronounced increase in body size from puberty to full adulthood—from 18 centimetres [Lp = 18 centimetres] to 55 centimetres [Li = 55 centimetres] in total length, and from approximately 80.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 80.7 grams] to approximately 2750 grams [Wwi = approximately 2750 grams] in wet weight—demonstrates the critical role of post-pubertal growth in maximizing the fecundity of larger, older females. The minute birth mass of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] underscores the extreme fecundity required to counterbalance the high mortality typical of pelagic larvae in the Gulf of Mexico, while the 15-year lifespan (15 years) [am = 15 years] allows for a cumulative reproductive output that buffers the population against environmental variability and supports sustainable harvest at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].
